title: Oil pumped into a tanker truck

stimulus.title: Oil pumped into a tanker truck
stimulus.text: Oil is pumped into a tanker truck at a rate $R(t)$ gallons per minute, where $t$ is measured in minutes. $R$ is differentiable and increasing on $0 \le t \le 12$. Selected values of $R(t)$ are shown in the table.

table.caption: Rate R(t), in gallons per minute, at selected times t, in minutes

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Use the data in the table to estimate $R'(4)$. Show the computations that lead to your answer. Indicate units of measure.

rubric.point: Answer $\frac{3}{2}$ gallons per minute per minute

parts.sample: $R'(4) \approx \frac{R(5) - R(3)}{5 - 3} = \frac{21 - 18}{2} = 1.5$ gallons per minute per minute.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Use a trapezoidal sum with the four subintervals indicated by the data in the table to approximate $\int_0^{12} R(t)\,dt$. Show the computations that lead to your answer.

rubric.point: A trapezoidal sum with the table's four widths 3, 2, 4 and 3

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Using correct units, explain the meaning of $\int_0^{12} R(t)\,dt$ in the context of the problem.

rubric.point: The number of gallons of oil pumped into the truck from $t = 0$ to $t = 12$ minutes
accept: must name the quantity (gallons of oil pumped in), the units (gallons) and the interval (0 to 12 minutes)

parts.sample: $\int_0^{12} R(t)\,dt$ is the total number of gallons of oil pumped into the tanker truck from $t = 0$ to $t = 12$ minutes.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A left Riemann sum with the four subintervals indicated by the table is used to approximate $\int_0^{12} R(t)\,dt$. Find its value, and explain whether it is an overestimate or an underestimate.

accept: must name R (or the rate) as increasing; "the graph goes up" alone earns nothing

parts.sample: Left sum $= 3(12) + 2(18) + 4(21) + 3(29) = 243$. Because $R$ is increasing on $[0, 12]$, on each subinterval $R$ is least at the left end, so each rectangle lies under the graph: 243 is an underestimate.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Must there be a value $t$, with $5 < t < 9$, for which $R'(t) = 2$? Justify your answer.

accept: the average rate of change over [5, 9] equals 2

rubric.point: Concludes yes by the Mean Value Theorem, stating that $R$ is differentiable (so continuous) on the interval
accept: "$R$ is differentiable, so it is continuous on $[5, 9]$ and differentiable on $(5, 9)$; by the MVT ..."

parts.sample: $R$ is differentiable, so $R$ is continuous on $[5, 9]$ and differentiable on $(5, 9)$. $\frac{R(9) - R(5)}{9 - 5} = \frac{29 - 21}{4} = 2$. By the Mean Value Theorem, there is a value $t$ with $5 < t < 9$ such that $R'(t) = 2$.
